title: A name from the Gayatri
hookLine: a childless king keeps offering with the Gayatri, and the daughter he is given carries its other name
carry: the Gayatri asks the light to wake our minds
last: TARPAN: WATER OFFERED TO THE ONES WE LOST.

lines: THE GAYATRI HAS A SECOND NAME.
cards: A verse with a second name. Earlier this year, the verse to the sun that people call the Gayatri turned up in the older law books as the Savitri, the verse to the god Savitr. Keep that name in your pocket.
In the Mahabharata, a sage sitting with the exiled Pandavas in the forest tells of a king with no child, and the verse he keeps offering with is that one. Last year we heard Savitri's whole story.
This time we stay with the woman herself, starting where she starts: with her name.

teach.b: The king is Ashvapati, ruler of the Madras. The epic calls him good, truthful and generous, and grieved by one thing: there is no child in his house. So he takes up a discipline.
He eats sparingly and keeps his senses in check. Again and again, into the sacred fire, he makes offerings with the Savitri verse, and he keeps it up a long time. Then one day the fire answers.

teach.h: THE GODDESS RISES FROM THE FIRE
teach.b: The goddess Savitri herself rises out of it, pleased with him, and offers him a gift. He asks for children. She tells him a daughter will be born to him, full of radiance.
When the girl comes, the king names her after the goddess who gave her: Savitri. Now the teaching, because this verse is the most well-known prayer in Hinduism.

teach.h: THE GAYATRI: MAY THE LIGHT STIR OUR THOUGHTS
teach.b: It's the Gayatri mantra, from the Rig Veda, and what it asks for, in paraphrase, is: may the light of the sun god stir our thoughts. Not wealth, not victory. A mind woken up.
That's why it's the verse a teacher whispers to a child at the sacred thread ceremony, and why the daily twilight rite, sandhya, says it at dawn and dusk, while the light is changing.

And the girl named for it grows into a woman who keeps her thinking clear under pressure: she chooses her husband, hears a terrible warning without flinching, and stands in front of Death and keeps talking.
The epic doesn't spell out the link; many readers hear it anyway. A prayer for a lit mind, made into a woman who keeps her head.

how: Hindus who keep the daily twilight rite, sandhya, recite the Gayatri, also called the Savitri, at dawn and dusk; it is the verse given at the sacred thread ceremony, and many families also sing or play it each morning.

s: in the epic, the princess is named after the goddess who granted her birth
the goddess Savitri rises from the fire, promises a daughter, and the king names the girl after her.
the Gayatri prays mainly for wealth and victory
it asks the sun god's light to stir our thoughts: a mind woken up.
the verse the law books call the Savitri is the one also known as the Gayatri
the same verse to the sun god Savitr goes by both names.

games.q: you're Ashvapati. after long years of offerings, the goddess Savitri rises from the fire and offers you a gift. what do you ask for?
games.why: children. she promises him a radiant daughter, and he names the girl after the goddess.

practice: Sit facing the light, a window or a lamp, and let it fall on your face for a few breaths. If you know the Gayatri and you pray, say it once, silently, the way it's said at dawn and dusk.
If you don't, ask in your own words for one clear thought today, and let the breath settle.

wordCard.voice: Savitri. A princess named for the goddess who rose from the fire, and for the Gayatri verse her father offered with. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the verse to the sun god Savitr, of the goddess who rose from the fire, and of the princess.

carryVoice: Your line: the Gayatri asks the light to wake our minds. Savitri was named for it. See you tomorrow.
